historical_timeline.summary: Born Sarah Breedlove in Delta, Louisiana, to formerly enslaved parents.
Both parents had died by the time she was seven.
Hair loss and scalp disease; began selling hair-care products as an agent.
Married Charles Joseph Walker in Denver and began her own company as Madam C. J. Walker.
Company moved to Indianapolis; thousands of agents trained.
Rest cure at Hot Springs, Arkansas, for her health; high blood pressure.
Joined the committee of the Negro Silent Protest Parade petitioning for a federal law against lynching.
Nephritis worsened by hypertension diagnosed; rest at Battle Creek advised.
Gravely ill in St. Louis; returned to New York.
Died at Villa Lewaro, Irvington-on-Hudson, at 51.

claims.statement: Madam C. J. Walker was born Sarah Breedlove on December 23, 1867, in Delta, Louisiana, the daughter of Owen and Minerva Anderson Breedlove. Both parents had been enslaved on a Madison Parish plantation, and she was their first child born into freedom.

Both her parents had died by the time she was seven, and she went to live with an older sister and moved across the river to Vicksburg, Mississippi. She married Moses McWilliams at fourteen, had her only child, Lelia (later A'Lelia), and was widowed at twenty. She then moved to St. Louis, where she worked as a laundress and cook, sometimes for as little as a dollar a day.
claims.clinical_interpretation: Anchors her early loss of both parents (cause not recorded) and the years of heavy physical work in the modern social history.

claims.statement: While working as a laundress she began to lose her hair, a problem many Black women of her time shared. Her biographers attribute it to scalp disease such as dandruff, poor diet, a hard life and harsh washing products, in an era when most homes lacked indoor plumbing. In 1904 she began using and selling another Black woman's hair grower as a sales agent, then developed her own sulfur-containing ointments and shampoos to treat scalp disease.
claims.clinical_interpretation: History only; the origin of her products. The modern episode adds no scalp or hair diagnosis.

source_links.locator: inspired by her own hair loss; sulfur ointments for scalp disease
her scalp was balding in patches; poor nutrition, a hard life and harsh treatments

claims.statement: In Denver she married Charles Joseph Walker, a newspaper advertising salesman (in January 1906, or 1905 in one account), and began calling herself Madam Walker, in part to avoid the familiar forms of address then used for Black women. She launched her own hair-care line there, set up headquarters and a training school for her agents in Pittsburgh in 1908, and moved the company to Indianapolis in 1910. She trained thousands of sales agents, "hair culturists," who earned a share of the profits. She kept the name after the marriage ended.
claims.clinical_interpretation: Anchors her chosen form of address and her work as a founder who trained agents and traveled constantly to sell and teach.

claims.statement: As her wealth grew she became a philanthropist and activist: she gave to the YWCA and paid tuition for students at Tuskegee Institute, and in 1915 she sued over discrimination at an Indianapolis theater.
claims.clinical_interpretation: Anchors her philanthropy and civic work in the modern social history.

source_links.locator: philanthropy and activism grew with her wealth

claims.statement: In 1917 she joined the committee of the Negro Silent Protest Parade in petitioning the President and Congress to make lynching a national crime. She gave $5,000 to the NAACP's anti-lynching work, and by her own report her company had more than twenty thousand agents by 1919.
claims.clinical_interpretation: History after the index date; anchors the later civic work and the size of her agent network.

source_links.locator: more than twenty thousand agents by 1919

claims.statement: The physical demands she placed on herself undermined her health, and she suffered from high blood pressure. She went for a rest cure at Hot Springs, Arkansas, in 1916, but otherwise did not slow her pace.
claims.clinical_interpretation: The anchor for the modern hypertension. The teaching contrast: the historical advice was to rest and slow down; the modern plan treats the blood pressure and fits care around the work she chooses.

developed health problems, including high blood pressure and kidney failure

claims.statement: By mid-November 1917 a Chicago physician, Dr. George Sauer, diagnosed nephritis, an often irreversible inflammation of the kidneys made worse by her worsening hypertension, and advised an indefinite stay at the Battle Creek Sanitarium in Michigan, where she took a rest cure that year.
claims.clinical_interpretation: History after the modern episode. Anchors the modern kidney disease; the modern kidney findings are synthetic.

source_links.locator: rest cure at Battle Creek Sanitarium in 1917

claims.statement: She moved into Villa Lewaro, her house at Irvington-on-Hudson, New York (in 1918; 1917 in one account). In April 1919 she became gravely ill in St. Louis and returned to New York.

source_links.locator: very ill on a trip to St. Louis in April 1919

claims.statement: She died on May 25, 1919, at Villa Lewaro, at 51. Accounts of the cause differ: chronic interstitial nephritis; kidney failure; or high blood pressure and kidney failure.
claims.clinical_interpretation: History only, two years after the modern episode. Anchors the hypertension and kidney disease.

synthetic_episode.teaching_objective: Hypertension with chronic kidney disease in a 49-year-old Black woman who founded and runs a national hair-care company and travels most weeks to train her sales agents. The episode covers accurate office measurement and 24-hour ambulatory and home monitoring under the 2025 AHA/ACC guideline; kidney function by the race-free CKD-EPI 2021 equation, stated explicitly, with the urine albumin-to-creatinine ratio, chronicity and KDIGO 2024 staging and risk; an angiotensin receptor blocker titrated to the maximum dose, an SGLT2 inhibitor for CKD with albuminuria, and a calcium channel blocker to reach goal; a statin chosen by shared decision; potassium and creatinine after each start or increase; sick-day rules tested by a real gastroenteritis; sodium counseling built on the food she likes; nephrology consultation; and a work and rest plan she sets herself. The teaching contrast is the historical advice to rest and slow down: here the risks are stated plainly, the treatment does the work, and she decides how she lives. Race and medicine: the eGFR uses no race term, the first medicine is chosen for the albuminuria rather than for her race, and APOL1 genetic testing is offered with counseling and left to her choice.

referral.question: Albumin in the urine (286 mg/g) and an eGFR of 54 by the race-free CKD-EPI 2021 equation in a 49-year-old woman with high blood pressure readings awaiting ambulatory confirmation, left ventricular hypertrophy on ECG and protein on a dipstick a year ago. Please advise on the cause, any further tests, kidney-protective treatment and her blood pressure target, APOL1 testing, and a monitoring plan that fits a schedule of travel most weeks
referral.urgency: Within two weeks, on the day of her two-week visit, so that she makes one trip
referral.pertinent_history: She founded and runs a hair-care company with a national network of sales agents and travels most weeks to train and speak. A workplace screening found high blood pressure; she has had morning headaches for some months. Her office has requested last year's executive physical results, which she recalls showed protein in the urine. No diabetes, no NSAID use, no kidney stones, no known family kidney disease; both parents died when she was a child. Today: blood pressure 166/102 (average of two readings), pulse 82, weight 79.0 kg, BMI 29.7. Fundi: mild arteriolar narrowing without hemorrhages. Results today: sodium 140, potassium 4.4, bicarbonate 25 mmol/L; creatinine 1.22 mg/dL, eGFR 54 (CKD-EPI 2021, race-free); glucose 94 mg/dL; A1c 5.4%; urine albumin-to-creatinine ratio 286 mg/g; urinalysis 1+ protein, no blood, bland sediment; total cholesterol 250, LDL 174, HDL 46, triglycerides 150 mg/dL; hemoglobin 12.4 g/dL; TSH 1.9. ECG: sinus rhythm, left ventricular hypertrophy by voltage criteria. Planned before your visit: 24-hour ambulatory monitoring and home readings, a repeat urine albumin and creatinine, calcium, phosphate, parathyroid hormone and 25-hydroxyvitamin D, and a kidney ultrasound on the morning of your visit. No medicines started yet

consultant_note.history: Madam Walker, 49, is seen at the request of Dr. Okonjo-Bell on the day of her two-week visit. She asked to be addressed as Madam Walker. Her ambulatory monitor showed a 24-hour mean of 149/94, daytime 154/98 and night 140/88, and her home readings average 152/96. Her office has sent last year's executive physical: creatinine 1.18 mg/dL and protein 1+ on a dipstick. She has had morning headaches on some days. She has no visible blood in the urine, no foamy urine she has noticed, no swelling, rash, joint pain, mouth ulcers or kidney stones, and takes no NSAIDs, supplements or herbal products. No known family kidney disease; both parents died when she was a child. She asked plainly whether she will need dialysis and said she would take whatever medicines were needed but would not give up her travel
consultant_note.data_reviewed: Dr. Okonjo-Bell's intake note and results: creatinine 1.22 mg/dL, eGFR 54 at intake and 1.21 mg/dL, eGFR 55 today (CKD-EPI 2021, race-free); potassium 4.4 mmol/L; urine albumin-to-creatinine ratio 286 mg/g at intake and 294 mg/g today; urinalysis 1+ protein without blood, bland sediment; calcium 9.4 mg/dL, phosphate 3.6 mg/dL, parathyroid hormone 58 pg/mL, 25-hydroxyvitamin D 31 ng/mL; A1c 5.4%; LDL 174 mg/dL; hemoglobin 12.4 g/dL. ECG: left ventricular hypertrophy by voltage. Kidney ultrasound this morning: right kidney 10.4 cm, left 10.6 cm, normal cortical thickness, mildly increased echogenicity, no hydronephrosis, stones or cysts. Ambulatory and home readings as above; clinic 160/100 today

exam.finding: Blood pressure 160/100 and pulse 80, measured by the clinic nurse today
Regular rhythm; sustained apex beat; no bruits

assessment.assessment: Albuminuria and a reduced eGFR present for more than a year: CKD G3a A2, high risk on the KDIGO heat map. Long-standing hypertension with left ventricular hypertrophy and retinopathy, a bland sediment without hematuria, albuminuria below 300 mg/g and normal-sized kidneys make hypertensive kidney disease the most likely cause. A primary glomerular disease is less likely, and a biopsy is not needed now. Her 5-year kidney failure risk is 1.6% (4-variable KFRE): low, and treatment can lower it further. The race-free equation stages her correctly; the older equation with a race coefficient would have reported an eGFR of about 60

Stage 2 hypertension confirmed by ambulatory monitoring, with a non-dipping pattern. With albuminuria, a renin-angiotensin blocker at the maximum tolerated dose is the foundation, chosen for the kidney disease and not for her race; an ARB avoids the cough of an ACE inhibitor, which matters for her work. Target below 130/80, and a systolic near 120 if she tolerates it with standardized measurement

recommendations: Losartan 50 mg each morning, increased to 100 mg after two weeks if potassium is below 5.5 mmol/L and creatinine has risen by less than 30%
Empagliflozin 10 mg daily for kidney protection, indicated at her eGFR and albuminuria without diabetes; expect a small early dip in eGFR
Sick-day rules: hold losartan and empagliflozin on days of vomiting, diarrhea or not eating, and restart after a day of normal eating and drinking
Potassium and creatinine two to four weeks after each start or increase, then every six months with the urine albumin; booking the draws on her days at home is acceptable
Amlodipine as the next medicine if blood pressure stays above goal on the maximum losartan dose; no potassium-based salt substitutes
Hepatitis B, hepatitis C and HIV tests now, as part of the evaluation of new CKD, and hepatitis B vaccination if she is not immune

APOL1 genotyping may be offered with genetic counseling: two high-risk variants raise the lifetime risk of kidney disease and help explain it, but the result would not change today's treatment; it is her choice whether and when to test
No biopsy now; reconsider for hematuria, albuminuria rising above 1,000 mg/g despite treatment, or an unexplained fall in eGFR of more than 30%
Avoid NSAIDs, and tell any clinician about her kidneys before contrast dye
consultant_note.communication: Discussed with Dr. Okonjo-Bell after the visit. The diagnosis, the low 5-year risk and each medicine were explained to Madam Walker with the numbers, and she agreed to start losartan and empagliflozin today. APOL1 testing was explained and written information given; she will decide later
consultant_note.follow_up: Nephrology review in about six months, by video if she prefers, or sooner for potassium above 5.5 mmol/L, a fall in eGFR of more than 30%, albuminuria rising, or blood pressure not at goal on three medicines; Dr. Okonjo-Bell continues care and monitoring
